# Programming your own API functions
## R Setup {.unnumbered}

```{r}
# Load necessary libraries
library(httr2)
library(Rilostat)
library(WDI)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Load the saved datasets
df_ilo <- readRDS("data/df_ilostat_womenparticipation.RDS")
df_wb <- readRDS("data/df_WorldBank_gdp_capita.RDS")
```

## Female labour force participation (ILO)

### Retrieve data using your own API wrapper

**Explanation of the URL.** Our function builds the URL from the ILO
SDMX endpoint `https://sdmx.ilo.org/rest/data/`, the dataflow with
agency and version `ILO,DF_EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT,1.0` and the data key,
whose dot-separated positions filter country, frequency (annual), sex
(women) and age group (45–54), with one position left empty (no
filter). Several countries are joined with "+", and an empty country
position returns all countries. The period `startPeriod`, `endPeriod`
and the CSV output format are then added as query parameters with
`req_url_query()`.

```{r}
get_ilodata <- function(country = "", year_from = 1950, year_to = 2025,
                        dataset_identifier = "DF_EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT") {

  # Check the inputs before sending anything
  if (!is.numeric(year_from) || !is.numeric(year_to) || year_from > year_to) {
    stop("year_from and year_to must be numbers with year_from <= year_to.",
         call. = FALSE)
  }

  # Several country codes are joined with "+"; an empty country position
  # means "all countries" in SDMX
  country <- paste(toupper(country), collapse = "+")

  # Path of the URL: endpoint, dataflow (agency, identifier, version) and
  # data key (country . frequency . (empty) . sex . age group)
  host_url <- "https://sdmx.ilo.org/rest/data/"
  agency <- "ILO"
  dataset_version <- "1.0"
  path_url <- paste0(host_url,
                     agency, ",", dataset_identifier, ",", dataset_version, "/",
                     country, ".A..SEX_F.AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54")

  # Query parameters: period and output format
  req <- request(path_url) |>
    req_url_query(startPeriod = year_from,
                  endPeriod = year_to,
                  dimensionAtObservation = "AllDimensions",
                  format = "csvfilewithlabels") |>
    req_timeout(60)

  # Own error message if the request does not come through (HTTP error like
  # 404/500, or no internet connection). The ILO also answers with an error
  # if a query simply has no data.
  resp <- tryCatch(
    req_perform(req),
    error = function(e) {
      stop("ILO API request failed for country '", country, "' (",
           year_from, "-", year_to, "): ", conditionMessage(e),
           call. = FALSE)
    }
  )

  # Read the CSV from the response and keep the columns we need
  df <- read.csv(text = resp_body_string(resp))

  if (nrow(df) == 0) {
    stop("ILO API returned no data for country '", country, "' (",
         year_from, "-", year_to, ").", call. = FALSE)
  }

  df <- df |>
    select("REF_AREA", "Reference.area", "Sex", "TIME_PERIOD", "OBS_VALUE") |>
    rename(Country_code = REF_AREA,
           Country = Reference.area,
           Gender = Sex,
           Year = TIME_PERIOD,
           Value = OBS_VALUE) |>
    mutate(Year = as.integer(Year))

  return(df)
}
```

We check the two other requirements of the function: without a country
it returns all countries, and for an invalid country it returns our own
error message.

```{r}
# No country specified: all countries, default period 1950-2025
ilo_all <- get_ilodata()

c(countries_api   = n_distinct(ilo_all$Country_code),
  countries_part1 = n_distinct(df_ilo$ref_area))

# Which codes are in only one of the two?
setdiff(unique(ilo_all$Country_code), unique(df_ilo$ref_area))
setdiff(unique(df_ilo$ref_area), unique(ilo_all$Country_code))

# Invalid country code
error_ilo <- tryCatch(
  get_ilodata(country = "XXX", year_from = 2023, year_to = 2023),
   error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
```

Without a country, our function returns data for
`r n_distinct(ilo_all$Country_code)` countries and territories, the same number
as in the Part 1 data `r n_distinct(df_ilo$ref_area)`, and no country code
appears in only one of the two. An invalid country code does not crash the
function: it returns our own error message "`r error_ilo`".

### Test your API

**1.** We apply our function to Switzerland, the USA and Germany for
2023, using `lapply()` over the country codes.

```{r}
countries <- c("CHE", "DEU")

ilo_own <- lapply(countries, function(x) {
  get_ilodata(country = x, year_from = 2023, year_to = 2023)
}) |>
  bind_rows()

ilo_own
```

The function returns one row per country with the participation rate
of women aged 45–54 in 2023: Switzerland
`r round(ilo_own$Value[ilo_own$Country_code == "CHE"], 1)` %, the USA
`r round(ilo_own$Value[ilo_own$Country_code == "USA"], 1)` % and Germany
`r round(ilo_own$Value[ilo_own$Country_code == "DEU"], 1)` %.

**2.** We run the same query with `Rilostat` and compare both results
on country code and year. We try Rilostat's default setting and the
setting from Part 1 `best_source = "all"`, because Part 1 showed that
one country can have several sources for the same year.

```{r}
ilo_filters <- list(
  ref_area = countries,
  sex = "SEX_F",
  classif1 = "AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54",
  timefrom = 2023,
  timeto = 2023
)

# Rilostat default
ilo_pkg <- get_ilostat(
  id = "EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A",
  type = "code",
  time_format = "num",
  filters = ilo_filters,
  quiet = TRUE
)

# Rilostat with all sources, as in Part 1
ilo_pkg_all <- get_ilostat(
  id = "EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A",
  type = "code",
  time_format = "num",
  filters = ilo_filters,
  best_source = "all",
  quiet = TRUE
)

# Rows per country and year: more than one row means several sources
count(ilo_pkg, ref_area, time)
count(ilo_pkg_all, ref_area, time)

# Compare our function with the Rilostat default
comparison_ilo <- full_join(
  ilo_own |> select(Country_code, Year, Value_api = Value),
  ilo_pkg |> select(Country_code = ref_area, Year = time,
                    Value_rilostat = obs_value, source),
  by = c("Country_code", "Year")
) |>
  mutate(Difference = Value_api - Value_rilostat)

comparison_ilo
```

Yes, the results are the same: for all three countries our function returns
exactly the values that Rilostat returns (largest absolute difference:
`r max(abs(comparison_ilo$Difference))`). Rilostat has exactly one value per
country and year in both settings (default and `best_source = "all"`), so the
choice of setting makes no difference here.

## Bonus: GDP per capita (World Bank)

### Import the data using your own API wrapper

```{r}
get_wbdata <- function(indicator = "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD", country = "all",
                       year_from = 1960, year_to = 2025) {

  # Several countries are separated by ";" in the World Bank API
  country <- paste(country, collapse = ";")

  # Country and indicator are two different path segments;
  # format = json, otherwise the API returns XML
  req <- request("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country") |>
    req_url_path_append(country, "indicator", indicator) |>
    req_url_query(format = "json",
                  date = paste0(year_from, ":", year_to),
                  per_page = 20000)   # all observations on one page

  resp <- tryCatch(
    req_perform(req),
    error = function(e) {
      stop("World Bank API request failed: ", conditionMessage(e),
           call. = FALSE)
    }
  )

  body <- resp_body_json(resp, simplifyVector = TRUE)

  # An invalid indicator still returns status 200, with an error message
  # instead of data: then there is no second element with data
  if (length(body) < 2 || length(body[[2]]) == 0) {
    stop("World Bank API returned no data for indicator '", indicator,
         "' and country '", country, "'.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  meta <- body[[1]]   # first element: page, pages, per_page, total
  data <- body[[2]]   # second element: the observations

  df <- tibble(
    Country_code = data$countryiso3code,
    Country_iso2 = data$country$id,
    Country      = data$country$value,
    Year         = as.integer(data$date),
    Value        = as.numeric(data$value)
  )

  # Check that all expected observations were received
if (nrow(df) != meta$total) {
  stop("Received ", nrow(df), " of ", meta$total, " observations.",
       call. = FALSE)
}

  return(df)
}
```

### Test your API

```{r}
wb_own <- lapply(countries, function(x) {
  get_wbdata(country = x, year_from = 2023, year_to = 2023)
}) |>
  bind_rows()

wb_own

wb_pkg <- WDI(country = c("CH", "US", "DE"), indicator = "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD",
              start = 2023, end = 2023)

comparison_wb <- full_join(
  wb_own |> select(Country_iso2, Year, Value_api = Value),
  wb_pkg |> select(Country_iso2 = iso2c, Year = year,
                   Value_wdi = NY.GDP.PCAP.KD),
  by = c("Country_iso2", "Year")
) |>
  mutate(Difference = Value_api - Value_wdi)

comparison_wb

# Invalid indicator: status 200, but our function returns an error message
error_wb <- tryCatch(
  get_wbdata(indicator = "NOT.AN.INDICATOR", country = "CHE"),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
```

Yes, the results are the same: for all three countries our function returns
exactly the values that `WDI` returns (largest absolute difference:
`r max(abs(comparison_wb$Difference))`), e.g. Switzerland
`r format(round(wb_own$Value[wb_own$Country_code == "CHE"]), scientific = FALSE)` US dollars in 2023. An
invalid indicator returns our own error message "`r error_wb`".

# Cleaning, merging and analysing the data

## First data exploration
### Structures and types

```{r}
# Inspect the structure and variable types
str(df_ilo)
str(df_wb)
```

The ILO dataset is a tibble with 4,535 rows and 12 columns in long format. Country/territory names, sources, indicator descriptions, sex, age groups and notes are character variables. The year `time`, participation rate `obs_value` and source flag `best_source` are numeric.

The World Bank dataset is a data frame with 17,556 rows and 5 columns in long format, including countries and regional aggregates. Country names and codes `country`, `iso2c`, `iso3c` are character variables, `year` is an integer, and GDP per capita `NY.GDP.PCAP.KD` is numeric.

### Describing the datasets

```{r}
# ILO test 1: check whether the sample contains only women aged 45–54
df_ilo |>
  count(sex, classif1)

# ILO test 2: multiple observations for the same country and year
df_ilo |>
  count(ref_area, time) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()
```
```{r}
# World Bank test 1: non-positive GDP per capita
df_wb |>
  filter(NY.GDP.PCAP.KD <= 0) |>
  nrow()

# World Bank test 2: missing GDP per capita
df_wb |>
  filter(is.na(NY.GDP.PCAP.KD)) |>
  nrow()
```
**ILO**

- **Definition:** The indicator measures the share of women aged 45–54 who are employed or unemployed, actively seeking work and available to work.
- **Units:** Percent of the female population aged 45–54.
- **Quality:** All 4,535 observations refer to women aged 45–54. However, 477 country-year combinations contain multiple observations, which require investigation during cleaning.
- **Unit of observation:** A reported participation rate for a country or territory in a given year, with source information. Country-year combinations are not always unique.
- **Time structure:** Annual panel data: countries and territories are observed repeatedly over time.

**World Bank**

- **Definition:** GDP per capita is gross domestic product divided by population.
- **Units:** Constant 2015 US dollars per person.
- **Quality:** No recorded GDP values are zero or negative, but 2,995 observations have missing GDP values.
- **Unit of observation:** A country or aggregate in a particular year.
- **Time structure:** Annual panel data, with repeated observations over time and missing GDP values for some country-year combinations.

## Data Cleaning

First we will inspect the ILO data; checking variable names and making sure that all constraints are met.

```{r}
# Checking the names of columns
colnames(df_ilo)
```

```{r}
# Checking if we only have the data for women aged 45-54
cat("Age range:", unique(df_ilo$classif1), "\n")
# Checking if the data has values by country
cat("Number of countries:", length(unique(df_ilo$ref_area)), "\n")
# Checking time restriction
cat("Date from:", min(df_ilo$time), "\n")
cat("Date to:", max(df_ilo$time))
```

The age and time constraints are met, however the number of countries is too high. Before adressing this issue we will take a look at the World Bank data:

```{r}
# Checking the names of columns
colnames(df_wb)
```

```{r}
# Checking if we only have the data for constant 2015 US dollars
cat("Attribute:", attr(df_wb$NY.GDP.PCAP.KD, "label"), "\n")
# Checking if the data has values by country
cat("Number of countries:", length(unique(df_wb$country)), "\n")
# Checking time restriction
cat("Date from:", min(df_wb$year), "\n")
cat("Date to:", max(df_wb$year))
```

The age and time constraints are met, however the number of countries is too high and there is no LOG variable. We will adress both of these issues later.

We will now move on to the task. Our goal is to create a minimal data frame or tibble with tha variables `country`, `date`, and `obs_value`.

First we want to learn why there are as many countries as shown above and remove any observations that do not meet our constraints.

```{r}
head(unique(df_ilo$ref_area),5)
```

We need to convert the country codes into the actual country names by creating a new object.

```{r}
# Labeling the ILO Data Frame
df_ilo_labeled <- label_ilostat(df_ilo)
# Checking the names of columns
colnames(df_ilo_labeled)
# Checking the country names
head(unique(df_ilo_labeled$ref_area.label),5)
```

It appears that the data indeed contain data per country. There are some countries on the list that have been dissolved since the respective data were captured, which is why the number is higher than expected.

We now want to remove any variables that are not relevant to our analysis. We will exclude `source.label`, `indicator.label`, `sex.label`, `classif1.label`, `obs_status.label`,`note_source.label`, `note_indicator.label` and `best_source` because they do not add any new information.

```{r}
df_ilo_labeled <- df_ilo_labeled |>
  select(ref_area.label,
         time,
         obs_value,
         note_classif.label)
glimpse(df_ilo_labeled)
```

All observations that are non-empty in the variable `note_classif.label` are noncompliant with our age constraint. Therefore we will exclude them from the dataset.

```{r}
df_ilo_labeled <- df_ilo_labeled |>
  filter(is.na(note_classif.label)) |>
  select(-note_classif.label)
glimpse(df_ilo_labeled)
```

Now we check if we have multiple observations for the same country and year and if there are empty rows.

```{r}
# ILO test: multiple observations for the same country and year
df_ilo_labeled |>
  count(ref_area.label, time) |>
  summarise(duplicates = sum(n - 1))

df_ilo_labeled |>
  filter(is.na(obs_value)) |>
  nrow()
```

There are no missing values and there are 510 instances where there is more than one observation per year for a given country. We take a closer look at the respective data to find out why. To do that, we create another object with the same data as `df_ilo_labeled`, but without the filters.

```{r}
# Create a labeled full data set
df_ilo_labeled_full <- label_ilostat(df_ilo)

# Show all instances where there are multiple year-value combinations for a given country
df_ilo_labeled_full_duplicates <- df_ilo_labeled_full |>
  semi_join(df_ilo_labeled, by = c("ref_area.label", "time", "obs_value")) |>
  group_by(ref_area.label, time) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  print()
```
We can now see the problem. Our data contains observations from multiple sources. So we want to find out if we can observe a pattern or if duplicates (or triplets and more) occur randomly. For that we use regular expressions to create an object that shows us which source-combinations happen and how many times they happen. The sum may be smaller than 510, because we count the number of redundant combinations, not the number of redundancies caused by those combinations.

```{r}
df_ilo_labeled_full_duplicates |>
  mutate(source = sub(" - .*", "", source.label)) |>
  group_by(ref_area.label, time) |>
  summarise(
    sources = paste(sort(source), collapse = " + "),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  count(sources, sort = TRUE)
```

There are 477 redundant source combinations. There are multiple patterns, so we need to find an abstract solution that will correct all flaws at once. We will prioritize Labour Force Survey (LFS) observations and retain only one observation per country-year combination. If no LFS observations are available, we will retain the first available observation from an alternative source.

```{r}
df_ilo_clean <- df_ilo_labeled_full |>
  filter(is.na(note_classif.label)) |>
  arrange(desc(startsWith(source.label, "LFS"))) |>
  distinct(ref_area.label, time, .keep_all = TRUE)


# Count duplicates
df_ilo_clean |>
  count(ref_area.label, time) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()
```

There are no more redundancies. To make sure that we didn't remove more than was needed, we take the difference of the number of rows in the old and new data frame and expect it to be 510.

```{r}
# Check if the difference between the rows in the old and cleaned data frames is 510
nrow(df_ilo_labeled) - nrow(df_ilo_clean)
```

The difference adds up to what we wanted, so now we select only relevant columns to clean it up.

```{r}
df_ilo_clean <- df_ilo_clean |>
  select(ref_area.label, time, obs_value)
df_ilo_clean
```

The female labour force participation rate dataset is now ready for analysis and stored in the object `df_ilo_clean`. It contains the minimal relevant data. 

Let's move on to the GDP per capita data. Our goal is to store an object that contains unique observations of the variables `country`, `year`, and `NY.GDP.PCAP.KD`.

We take a glimpse into the dataset to find any obvious anomalies:

```{r}
glimpse(df_wb)
```
We can see that the data contain some geographic areas that are not countries. We wil filter them out by creating a variable with all [World Bank iso3c country codes](https://wits.worldbank.org/wits/wits/witshelp/content/codes/country_codes.htm) and selecting them.

```{r}
df_wb_countries <- df_wb |>
  filter(iso3c %in% wb_iso3c)

glimpse(df_wb_countries)
```
Now we check if there are any redundant entries.

```{r}
df_wb_countries |>
  count(iso3c, year) |>
  summarise(redundancies = sum(n - 1))
```
There are no redundancies here. Finally we will count the number of `NA` values in the GDP data, so that we can fill them up.

```{r}
# Count missing GDP values
sum(is.na(df_wb_countries$NY.GDP.PCAP.KD))

# Estimating missing values
df_wb_clean <- df_wb_countries |>
  arrange(iso3c, year) |>
  group_by(iso3c) |>
  fill(NY.GDP.PCAP.KD, .direction = "downup") |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(country, iso3c, year, gdp_capita = NY.GDP.PCAP.KD)

# Select relevant variables
df_wb_clean <- df_wb_countries |>
  select(country, iso3c, year, gdp_capita = NY.GDP.PCAP.KD)

# Check remaining missing values
sum(is.na(df_wb_clean$gdp_capita))

```

According to findings from a quick research, this suggests that the countries with missing values have no data at all. Let's verify:

```{r}
df_wb_countries |>
  group_by(country, iso3c) |>
  summarise(
    total = n(),
    missing = sum(is.na(NY.GDP.PCAP.KD)),
    non_missing = sum(!is.na(NY.GDP.PCAP.KD)),
    missing_pct = round(missing / total * 100, 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(missing > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(missing))
```

This suspicion was falsified, so we need an alternative heuristic to deal with the NAs. We will drop all countries out of the list that have more than 30% missing observations. This makes sure that we maintain data quality, without disproportionately excluding developing countries.

```{r}
threshold <- 0.30

df_wb_clean <- df_wb_countries |>
  group_by(country, iso3c) |>
  filter(mean(is.na(NY.GDP.PCAP.KD)) <= threshold) |>
  ungroup()
glimpse(df_wb_clean)
sum(is.na(df_wb_clean$NY.GDP.PCAP.KD))
```

The number of missing values has been reduced. There are several ways to fill out the missing observations.

We could use Interpolation (for missing values in between existing observations), extrapolation (for missing values at the start and end of the time series), or forward/backward filling (for all, as was tried earlier) to deal with the remaining values. However extrapolation assumes constant growth trends in GDP per capita, which is hard to reconcile with macroeconomic theory (across countries). Therefore we will drop the remaining countries with missing values (NAs), since they only make up 4.42% of the dataset. We must keep this limitation in mind when making general statements in our conclusion.

```{r}
df_wb_clean <- df_wb_clean |>
  group_by(iso3c) |>
  filter(!any(is.na(NY.GDP.PCAP.KD))) |>
  ungroup()

sum(is.na(df_wb_clean$NY.GDP.PCAP.KD))

glimpse(df_wb_clean)
```

There are no more missing values, so now we select only relevant columns to clean it up.

```{r}
df_wb_clean <- df_wb_clean |>
  select(country, year, NY.GDP.PCAP.KD)
df_wb_clean
```

GDP per capita in constant 2015 US dollars dataset is now ready for analysis and stored in the object df_wb_clean. It contains the minimal relevant data.

As hinted in the exercise, we are later required to merge the datasets `df_ilo_clean`and `df_wb_clean` later. Therefore it may be practical to only keep countries in `df_ilo_clean` that are in the also in the World Bank dataset and also check whether the datasets contain identical countries. If not, those outliers will also be filtered out. For the same reason it may be sensible to only include observations that start in 1960 in the ILO data.

First we identify countries that do not match.

```{r}
# Countries only in the ILO dataset
head(setdiff(df_ilo_clean$ref_area.label, df_wb_clean$country),5)

# Countries only in the World Bank dataset
setdiff(df_wb_clean$country, df_ilo_clean$ref_area.label)
```

Now we retain common countries.

```{r}
df_ilo_clean <- df_ilo_clean |>
  semi_join(df_wb_clean, by = c("ref_area.label" = "country")) |>
  mutate(time = as.integer(time))

df_wb_clean <- df_wb_clean |>
  semi_join(df_ilo_clean, by = c("country" = "ref_area.label"))

glimpse(df_ilo_clean)
glimpse(df_wb_clean)
```

And finally we verify that the countries are identical.

```{r}
setequal(df_ilo_clean$ref_area.label, df_wb_clean$country)
```

The data are now ready for the next part and stored in the objects `df_ilo_clean` and `df_wb_clean`.
